claims.claim: Default user-facing responses run longer than prior Opus models, and effort controls how much the model thinks rather than how much it says, so lowering effort does not reliably shorten the visible response; prompt for conciseness explicitly.
claims.note: The effort-is-not-a-length-lever distinction is the actionable half: a reader who reaches for effort to shorten output will not get it.

claims.claim: In a long system prompt, pair the conciseness instruction with a short reminder near the end of the prompt.

This model narrates readily during agentic work and its per-message output in agentic sessions is often longer than prior models'; describe the cadence and shape of updates you want, and prefer positive examples of the style over instructions about what not to do.

Files this model writes to disk (reports, Markdown documents, summaries) are often longer than on prior models, separately from conversational verbosity, so add explicit length calibration for Claude-authored documents.

This model verifies its own work without being told to, so REMOVE explicit verification instructions and legacy harness verification scaffolding: they cause over-verification, and removing them reduces wasted tokens with no loss in quality.
claims.note: Nexus-Hub intentionally retains the model-independent [[verification-before-completion]] claim-evidence gate: run the narrowest fresh evidence set that covers the claim, but omit unconditional duplicate self-check prompts and verifier subagents. Decision: docs/decisions/implemented/process/2026-09-24-retain-claim-evidence-for-opus-5.md. Deliberately scoped model-specific; this profile does not edit the shared body.

claims.claim: This model can expand the scope of a task, adding steps that were not requested; for narrow tasks constrain scope explicitly and tell it to stop short of actions clearly beyond what was asked.

This model delegates to subagents more readily than prior models; give explicit criteria for which scenarios warrant delegation, or set deterministic caps, because delegation multiplies cost and time when applied to small tasks.
claims.note: On Claude Code and the Agent SDK the deterministic caps are CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH, CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS, and the SDK's max_budget_usd, requiring Claude Code 2.1.217 or later. Claude Code adds its own delegation instruction on this model only under the claude_code system-prompt preset.

claims.claim: This model catches and fixes its own mistakes well without prompting, so avoid instructing re-checks such as "double-check your answer" or "re-verify before responding": they compound with the model's own behavior and add cost without improving results.

This model narrates corrections to its earlier statements more than prior models; limit correction narration to errors that would change the user's code, conclusions, or decisions, and make silent fixes for slips that change nothing.

In code review this model may follow a "only report high-severity issues" or "be conservative" instruction literally and report less; ask it to report everything and filter in a separate pass instead.

`low` and `medium` effort produce strong quality at a fraction of the tokens and latency of higher settings and accuracy holds at lower effort; start at the default `high`, use `low` and `medium` liberally where quality holds, step up to `xhigh` for demanding agentic work, and re-run an effort sweep if defaults were carried over from a prior model.

Thinking is on by default and can be disabled only at effort `high` or below; keep thinking enabled and control cost with lower effort instead, because thinking enabled at `low` effort performs better than thinking disabled at similar cost.
claims.note: With thinking disabled two artifacts can appear: a tool call written as user-facing text that never runs (and persists in agentic history), and internal XML tags leaking into the reply. A general instruction mitigates both; instructions that name thinking tags specifically are less effective.

claims.claim: Callers that used the none or minimal reasoning effort should start with low and compare results; GPT-6 Astra does not support the none reasoning effort.
claims.note: Confirmed verbatim on the guide and in the 2026-09-03 changelog entry on the second, refutation-oriented fetch.

claims.claim: When an application changes reasoning effort between responses in a standard single-agent request, use configuration_update items rather than a new conversation.
claims.note: Guide: 'If your application changes effort between responses, use configuration_update items in standard, single-agent requests.' The changelog adds that effort can change mid-conversation while preserving cached prompt prefixes.

claims.claim: Chat Completions is supported, but tool calling requires the Responses API.
claims.note: Guide: 'GPT-6 Astra supports Chat Completions, but tool calling requires Responses.' Changelog: 'Tool calling requires the Responses API.'

claims.claim: Async tools are enabled by setting async: true on a function or custom tool and returning the result when ready using the original call_id.
claims.note: Confirmed on the guide; the changelog lists async tool calling among the long-running-work controls.

claims.claim: Remove temperature, top_p, and top_logprobs from requests; the model does not accept custom sampling parameters or log probabilities.
claims.note: Guide: 'Remove temperature, top_p, and top_logprobs.' Changelog: no custom temperature or top_p values or log probabilities.

claims.claim: Fast mode carries no latency SLA, and service_tier fast is not supported with EU data residency.
claims.note: Guide: 'Fast mode for GPT-6 Astra does not include a latency SLA' and does not support service_tier fast with EU data residency.

claims.claim: Replace prompt_cache_retention with prompt_cache_options.ttl set to 30m.
claims.note: Confirmed verbatim on the guide.

claims.claim: Treat a user prompt that requests action, such as one phrased 'can you...', as an instruction to do the work rather than a question about capability.
claims.note: The platform-agnostic form of this rule landed in the v4.7.0 Autonomous Operation block with this page cited as a second source; this claim records the vendor's own statement for this model.

claims.claim: The user's instructions take precedence over guidelines provided in a skill.
claims.note: Adopted platform-agnostically in the v4.7.0 Autonomous Operation block; recorded here as the vendor statement for this model.

claims.claim: Do not write tests for reversible, low-impact changes that mirror the implementation.
claims.note: Adopted platform-agnostically as the test-scope restraint rule owned by minimal-construction; recorded here as the vendor statement for this model.

claims.claim: The vendor instructs the model to parallelize work by delegating tasks to another agent whenever it can.
claims.note: Recorded and deliberately NOT adopted into any shared body: the catalog's agent-orchestration-primitives overrides it with the named-problem escalation gate.

claims.claim: Released September 3, 2026 as the vendor's most capable model for the hardest end-to-end work; the models catalog lists it among the flagship models with no access gate on 2026-09-05.
claims.note: Changelog 2026-09-03: 'Released GPT-6 Astra, our most capable model, built for the hardest end-to-end work.' The Codex CLI's live enumeration (codex debug models) did not list this id on 2026-09-05; see the v4.7 known-gaps ledger. Changelog: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/changelog

claims.claim: Start at the default effort level `high`, then sweep `low`, `medium`, `xhigh`, and `max` against your own evals; effort is the primary control for trading intelligence against latency and cost.
claims.note: Stated directly on the model's own prompting page. Model-specific because the page frames effort as this model's primary control and its level semantics as not transferable.

claims.claim: Re-run the effort sweep even if one was already run on Claude Fable 5, because effort level names do not correspond to the same amount of thinking across models.
claims.note: The non-transferability is itself the claim, so it cannot be generalized to a shared body.

claims.claim: At `medium` effort this model roughly matches Claude Fable 5 at lower cost, and at `low` it is often competitive with Opus and Sonnet models on cost per task while scoring higher, so include `low` wherever a smaller model at higher effort would otherwise be used.
claims.note: Confidence medium rather than high: the comparison is a vendor performance claim about their own models, not a mechanical behavior a reader can verify from the page itself.

claims.claim: This model writes fewer user-facing updates during long tool-calling turns than Claude Fable 5, more pronounced at higher effort and in longer tool chains.

Before adding prompt text asking for progress updates, first confirm the client actually requests them: progress notes arrive as progress-update `thinking` blocks and are empty under the default `thinking.display` of `omitted`, so set `display: "updates"` or `"summarized"`.
claims.note: Ordering matters and is the point: the page says to check the transport before editing the prompt, because a prompt fix cannot surface blocks the client never asked for.

claims.claim: Audit the prompt for legacy lines that suppress narration (such as "hold all findings for the final response") and remove them before adding any instruction asking for updates.
Append each assistant turn to the conversation history exactly as the API returned it, thinking blocks included, and do not edit earlier turns between requests.
claims.note: For accounts created on or after 2026-08-31 a replayed thinking block whose prefix changed returns 400, or drops the block under `prefix_mismatch_behavior: "drop_block"`. The page states future models are expected to enforce this for all accounts, but that is an expectation about other models and is deliberately not recorded as a shared-body claim.

claims.claim: Send per-turn reminders as turn-scoped system messages and change instructions or tools with a mid-conversation system message rather than rewriting `system` or `tools`, because in-place history edits both trip the thinking-block prefix check and restart the prompt cache.

This model's prose can be denser than Claude Fable 5's, with longer sentences and fewer paragraph breaks; an instruction that defines mannered prose as the anti-pattern helps, and the short form "Please remove all mannered prose" also tends to work.

This model uses bold less and is less likely to reach for headers, lists, or quotation marks than earlier models, so remove legacy anti-formatting rules and replace them with a rule stating when specific formatting is appropriate.
claims.note: The actionable half is a REMOVAL of prompt text written for a previous generation, which is the opposite of the usual add-an-instruction fix.

claims.claim: When summarizing documents this model is more likely than Claude Fable 5 to reproduce source passages without marking them as quotations; add one complete correct example to the system prompt containing the request, the response, and a rationale sentence.

On complex asynchronous workloads, add a system-prompt block telling the model it is operating autonomously and must not end its turn on a plan, a question, or a promise about work it has not done; the opening sentence stating the user is not watching carries much of the effect.
claims.note: Scoped model-specific despite reading like general advice, per the ambiguity-resolves-to-model-specific rule. Nexus-Hub already ships equivalent text as the `## Autonomous Operation` and `Delivering work` blocks added in v4.7.0, so no shared-body edit is proposed: the shared surface already carries it.

claims.claim: This model sometimes delivers more than the task asked for (fixing nearby code, extending unmentioned behavior, committing extra test files); an explicit instruction about what to leave out substantially reduces unrequested additions and committed test code with no measurable change in task success.

At `low` effort this model calls search and retrieval tools less often and is more likely to answer from memory; raising effort for the affected turns is often simpler than a prompt change, and otherwise a verification nudge treats an unfamiliar name as the thing to search.

Safeguard false positives are more likely with compile-check phrasing (ask "are there any bugs" rather than "does this compile without errors"), with lesser-known programming languages, and when tools return base64-encoded data into context.
claims.note: The page also states that finding vulnerabilities in source code is permitted and that a blocked request returns `stop_reason: "refusal"`.

claims.claim: This model is more likely than Claude Fable 5 to rewrite an entire file for a small change; an instruction to minimize edit tokens and prefer surgical edits restores the earlier behavior for small and medium changes.

At `xhigh` and especially `max` effort this model can draft a long deliverable in its thinking and then write it out again as the reply; run such requests at `high` unless a quality gain is measured, set `max_tokens` to cover thinking plus reply, and append the note explaining that both share one limit.

When this model delegates to subagents, do not force the lead agent to wait for each one: have the start-subagent tool return immediately, pass each result back in a later `user` message, and give the lead a separate tool to call when it wants to wait.
claims.note: Confidence medium: the page reports lower average time to completion at similar quality and cost, and also notes the model still often chooses to wait, so the gain is described as coming from a subset of runs.

claims.claim: This model calibrates response length to task complexity rather than defaulting to a fixed verbosity, giving shorter answers on simple lookups and longer ones on open-ended analysis; tune prompts if the product depends on a specific verbosity, and prefer positive examples of the concision you want over instructions about what not to do.
Effort defaults to `high`; raise to `xhigh` for the hardest coding and agentic tasks, and reserve `low` for short scoped or latency-sensitive work that is not intelligence-sensitive.

As a rough migration mapping, this model at `medium` is comparable to Claude Sonnet 4.6 at `high`, and at `high` comparable to Sonnet 4.6 at `max`; when benchmarking, match by observed thinking length rather than by effort name.

This model respects effort levels strictly, especially at the low end: at `low` and `medium` it scopes work to what was asked rather than going above and beyond, with some risk of under-thinking on moderately complex tasks at `low`; raise effort rather than prompting around shallow reasoning.

Adaptive thinking is on by default, a change from Claude Sonnet 4.6 where the same requests ran without thinking; disable entirely with `thinking: {type: "disabled"}`, and revisit `max_tokens` because it is a hard limit on thinking plus response text.
Manual extended thinking (`thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}`) is not supported and returns a 400 error; use adaptive thinking with the effort parameter instead.
This model uses a new tokenizer that produces approximately 30% more tokens for the same text, so `max_tokens` limits tuned for Claude Sonnet 4.6 may truncate equivalent output.

Setting `temperature`, `top_p`, or `top_k` to a non-default value returns a 400 error, which is new for Sonnet-class models; remove those parameters when migrating and steer tone through system-prompt instructions instead.

This model is more agentic than Claude Sonnet 4.6 and reaches for tools and self-verification loops more readily; with thinking disabled it is LESS likely to reach for tools, so add an explicit nudge if tool calls matter with thinking off. Higher effort (`high`, `xhigh`) shows substantially more tool usage.

This model provides regular, higher-quality user-facing updates through long agentic traces, so REMOVE scaffolding that forces interim status messages (such as "after every 3 tool calls, summarize progress").

This model interprets prompts literally and explicitly, particularly at lower effort: it does not silently generalize an instruction from one item to another and does not infer unmade requests, so state scope explicitly (for example "apply this to every section, not just the first").

On open-ended frontend and design briefs this model may settle into a consistent default visual style, and generic negative instructions shift it to a different fixed palette rather than producing variety; specify a concrete alternative direction, or have the model propose several directions before building.
claims.note: Because `temperature` is not accepted on this model, propose-options-first is the documented way to get meaningfully different design directions across runs.

claims.claim: A code-review harness tuned for an earlier model may show lower measured recall on this model because it follows "only report high-severity issues" more faithfully; ask for coverage at the finding stage and move confidence filtering to a separate step.
claims.note: The page is explicit that this is a harness effect rather than a capability regression: same investigation depth, fewer investigations converted into reported findings.

claims.claim: For coding or reasoning tasks on Haiku 4.5, consider enabling manual extended thinking with thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}; this is conditional, not a universal default.
claims.note: Three independent refutation lenses on 2026-09-25: currency and actionability survived; source support survived after quoting enabled. A complete live Claude roster remains unavailable, so this claim-only write preserves the 2026-09-08 roster metadata.

claims.claim: When migrating from GPT-5.5 or GPT-5.4 with a reasoning effort above none, compare the existing effort with one level lower on representative tasks.
claims.note: OpenAI frames this as GPT-5.6-family guidance, not a Sol-only difference. For a previous effort of none, its separate guidance keeps none as the latency baseline and tests low where reasoning or tool use may help. Three independent refutation reviews agreed on this boundary.

claims.claim: When migrating from GPT-5.5 or GPT-5.4 with a reasoning effort above none, compare the existing effort with one level lower on representative tasks.
claims.note: OpenAI frames this as GPT-5.6-family guidance, not a Luna-only difference. Test quality, latency, and cost for Luna separately; the source does not promise equivalent quality at lower effort. For prior effort none, retain none as the latency baseline and test low when reasoning or tool use may help. Three independent refutation reviews confirmed applicability and this boundary.

claims.claim: When migrating from GPT-5.5 or GPT-5.4 with a reasoning effort above none, compare the existing effort with one level lower on representative tasks.
claims.note: OpenAI frames this as GPT-5.6-family guidance, not a Terra-only difference. Test quality, latency, and cost for Terra separately; the source does not promise equivalent quality at lower effort. For prior effort none, retain none as the latency baseline and test low when reasoning or tool use may help. Three independent refutation reviews confirmed applicability and this boundary.

claims.claim: Effort levels are recalibrated on Claude Sonnet 5.5, so a level does not produce the same amount of thinking as on Claude Sonnet 5; re-run an effort sweep against your own evals instead of carrying the old setting over. The default on the Claude API is high.
claims.note: Quote: "Its levels are recalibrated: a level doesn't produce the same amount of thinking as the same level on Claude Sonnet 5." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: Start agentic coding and multistep tool use at medium for well-specified tasks and move to high for harder or longer ones; start chat and other latency-sensitive work at medium or low.
claims.note: Quote: "For agentic coding and multistep tool use, start at `medium` for well-specified tasks and move to `high` for harder or longer ones." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: Thinking counts toward max_tokens even when thinking content is not returned, so size max_tokens for thinking plus the reply; for agentic coding set max_tokens to 128,000, the model maximum, and stream the response.
claims.note: Quote: "Thinking counts toward `max_tokens` even when thinking content isn't returned to you." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: To get less thinking, lower the effort level; asking the model in the system prompt to think less does not reliably reduce its thinking.
claims.note: Quote: "Asking it in the system prompt to think less doesn't reliably reduce its thinking." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: Changing the top-level effort value between requests invalidates the prompt cache; to vary effort per turn while keeping the cache, use a per-message effort change (beta), which needs adaptive thinking.
claims.note: Quote: "Changing the top-level `effort` value between requests invalidates the prompt cache." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: thinking type between_tools is the lowest thinking setting and is accepted only at high effort or below; at xhigh or max effort a request with between_tools returns a 400 error.
claims.note: Quote: "At `xhigh` or `max` effort, a request with `between_tools` returns a 400 error." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: With between_tools, effort cannot change mid-conversation: a per-message output_config.effort that differs from the level in effect returns a 400 error; use adaptive thinking to vary effort per turn.
claims.note: Quote: "With `between_tools`, effort also can't change mid-conversation" Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: between_tools takes no other field: sending display, budget_tokens, or block_binding with it returns a 400 error.
claims.note: Quote: "`between_tools` takes no other field: `display`, `budget_tokens`, or `block_binding` sent with it returns a 400 error." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: With between_tools, remove any instruction that tells the model not to think, because such instructions make it more likely to write internal XML tags in its visible output.
claims.note: Quote: "Such instructions make it more likely that the model writes internal XML tags in its visible output." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: For a JSON answer to a task that needs a few steps of working out, with adaptive thinking, ending the system prompt with the line 'Think the problem through before you answer.' makes the model think before answering more often. It has no effect under between_tools in a request without tools.
claims.note: Quote: "With this line, the model more often thinks before it answers." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: With structured outputs at low and medium effort the model occasionally keeps thinking until max_tokens; treat any response whose stop_reason is max_tokens as failed, even if its text holds valid JSON, and retry.
claims.note: Quote: "Treat any response whose `stop_reason` is `"max_tokens"` as failed, even if its text holds valid JSON, and retry." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: Without structured outputs, parse the last complete JSON value in the text blocks rather than everything from the first opening brace to the last closing brace, because the model occasionally writes a draft before its final JSON.
claims.note: Quote: "Don't take everything from the first `{` to the last `}`." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: On agentic coding at low and medium effort the model sometimes checks in before the work is done: it may pause to confirm a plan, ask a question it could answer itself, or stop after one part of a multipart task. Try a higher effort level first; otherwise a system-prompt instruction to keep working until everything asked for is done, and to stop only when it cannot go on without the user or before a risky step, makes it carry more of the work through, so sessions at those levels run longer and cost more.
claims.note: Quote: "It might pause to confirm a plan, ask a question it could answer itself, or stop after one part of a multipart task to ask whether to continue." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 2 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: The model tends to add unrequested tests, documentation, and small supporting files that fit the repository's conventions, at every effort level and more at higher effort, while the requested change itself stays close to what was asked. A system-prompt instruction to stop and report once the requested work is done and checked, and to mention rather than make unrequested additions, reduces these additions at xhigh and max effort.
claims.note: Quote: "At `xhigh` and `max` effort, that paragraph reduces these additions and makes changes smaller overall." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 2 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: At xhigh and max effort the model can start its own rounds of review and verification after finishing a task, sometimes with reviewer subagents, and make related fixes it noticed; this takes more time and tokens, so run routine work at high or below, where it is rare.
claims.note: Quote: "This takes more time and tokens, so run routine work at `high` or below, where it's rare." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 2 (2/3 survived). Caveat raised in verification: the vendor says subagents are used only if the harness provides them.

claims.claim: A system-prompt instruction to stop and report once the requested work is done and its checks pass, without starting extra review or hardening rounds or launching reviewer subagents unless a review was asked for, makes self-started review rounds less frequent but does not remove them entirely. In vendor testing on coding tasks at max effort it stopped reviewer subagents and cut session cost by about a third with no change in quality.
claims.note: Quote: "It makes self-started review rounds by the main agent less frequent but doesn't remove them entirely." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 2 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: On an open-ended request the model can start building a deliverable when only ideas were wanted; say in the request or the system prompt that ideas or a plan come first.
claims.note: Quote: "If you want ideas or a plan first, say so in the request, or add this to your system prompt:" Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: Between tool calls, notes longer than a sentence or two come back as progress-update thinking blocks whose text is empty at the default display, so a client that renders only text blocks looks silent during a long agentic turn. With adaptive thinking, set display to updates (beta header thinking-display-updates-2026-08-18) to show them; with between_tools the notes already come back with their summary text and no display field may be sent.
claims.note: Quote: "With `between_tools`, the notes come back with their summary text, so no `display` field is needed." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 2 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: If long tool-calling turns stay quiet, the harness can count consecutive tool-calling steps with no user-facing text and, after several (for example five), append a one-turn reminder as a turn-scoped system message; stop after the second or third reminder and leave each reminder in messages.
claims.note: Quote: "If the turn stays quiet, stop sending reminders after the second or third." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: A genuine user message that arrives right after a tool result, or inside a tool_result block, can be treated as a possible prompt injection; never put user text inside a tool_result block, and deliver mid-turn user input as a user text block after the last tool_result.
claims.note: Quote: "Never put user text inside a `tool_result` block. The model misreads that placement most often." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: In interactive sessions where users can type mid-turn, do not add a token or budget countdown after tool results, and keep harness notices in a separate mid-conversation system message after the user's words.
claims.note: Quote: "In interactive sessions where users can type mid-turn, don't add your own token or budget countdown after tool results." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: At low effort the model sometimes reports a code change as done without running a check that exercises it. A system-prompt instruction to run a real check that exercises the change before reporting it done (the project's tests, type-checker, or build, or the changed command itself; a syntax-only check does not count), and to say which check was not run and why when none can run, makes skipped or superficial checks rare at low effort for only a slightly higher cost per task.
claims.note: Quote: "At `low` effort, it makes skipped or superficial checks rare, with no measurable change in task quality and only a slightly higher cost per task:" Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 2 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: The model occasionally calls a declared tool by a name that differs only in letter case, or passes a known parameter under a slightly different name; accept the call when the match is unambiguous, or return an is_error tool_result that states the exact expected name.
claims.note: Quote: "Claude Sonnet 5.5 occasionally calls a declared tool by a name that differs only in letter case, such as `bash` for `Bash`." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: On chat and knowledge-work tasks the model sometimes answers from training knowledge when a search would catch changed details; remove prompt language that discourages tool use and, if a search tool exists, instruct the model to check specifics that may have changed.
claims.note: Quote: "First, check your prompt for language that discourages tool use, such as "only use tools when strictly necessary" or "minimize tool calls", and remove it." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: For dense charts and technical drawings, give the model a tool to crop, zoom, or run code on the image; on charts this helps at every effort level, on technical drawings only from high effort up.
claims.note: Quote: "For dense charts and technical drawings, give Claude Sonnet 5.5 a way to crop, zoom, or run code on the image." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: A safety-classifier decline arrives as a normal response with stop_reason refusal, and stop_details.category names one of cyber, bio, frontier_llm, reasoning_extraction, or general_harms; benign work can also trigger general_harms.
claims.note: Quote: "`general_harms`: the request falls under another usage-policy area. Benign work can also trigger this category." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 2 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: Server-side fallback (beta, Claude API only) retries cyber and frontier_llm declines on Claude Sonnet 5 as the fallback model; it does not retry bio, reasoning_extraction, or general_harms declines.
claims.note: Quote: "(`fallbacks: "default"`, beta, Claude API only)" Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 2 (2/3 survived). Caveat raised in verification: fallback is enabled with fallbacks: "default" on the request.

claims.claim: Remove prompt instructions that ask the model to include its reasoning in the response, because they invite reasoning_extraction declines; with adaptive thinking, read the reasoning from summarized thinking blocks (display summarized) instead.
claims.note: Quote: "If your prompts ask the model to include its reasoning in the response, remove those instructions, because they invite `reasoning_extraction` declines." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 2 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: The Claude API model id is claude-sonnet-5-5, which has no date suffix.
claims.note: Quote: "Replace your model ID with `claude-sonnet-5-5`, which has no date suffix." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: Breaking change from Claude Sonnet 5: a tool_choice of type any or tool is rejected with a 400 error, including on the token counting endpoint. Send tool_choice auto and say in the prompt when to use the tool, because the model can then answer without calling it.
claims.note: Quote: "The model can then answer without calling the tool, so say in the prompt when to use it." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 3 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: To keep tool input schema-valid under tool_choice auto, mark the tool strict: true. Strict tool use supports a subset of JSON Schema and needs additionalProperties: false on every object, a request can carry at most 20 strict tools, and the MCP, computer use, and browser use toolset entries do not accept strict. On Amazon Bedrock strict tool use is not available for Claude Sonnet 5.5, so send auto without strict and validate the tool input in code.
claims.note: Quote: "A request can have at most 20 strict tools, and the MCP, computer use, and browser use toolset entries don't accept `strict`." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 3 (2/3 survived). Caveat raised in verification: in a longer tools list, mark only the tools that need strict.

claims.claim: Breaking change from Claude Sonnet 5: Claude Sonnet 5.5 reads thinking blocks from Claude Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8, Haiku 4.5, and earlier models but not from Claude Opus 5, Opus 5.5, or any Fable or Mythos model; the API drops blocks it cannot read, the request still returns 200, and dropped blocks are not billed.
claims.note: Quote: "The API drops blocks the model can't read." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 2 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: Each Claude Sonnet 5.5 thinking block is bound to what came before it: the system prompt, the tools, and earlier messages. By default, for accounts created on or after 2026-08-31 00:00 UTC on the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, and Google Cloud, replaying a block after such a change returns a 400 error. With adaptive thinking, sending the thinking-binding-controls-2026-08-01 beta header with thinking.block_binding.prefix_mismatch_behavior set to drop_block drops the affected blocks instead; on older accounts, setting that field opts the request into the check. With between_tools, keep the history append-only or strip the thinking blocks from the edited turn on.
claims.note: Quote: "To drop the affected blocks instead, send the `thinking-binding-controls-2026-08-01` beta header and set `thinking.block_binding.prefix_mismatch_behavior` to `"drop_block"`." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 3 (2/3 survived). Caveat raised in verification: on older accounts either value of the field opts the request in, and the main remedy is an append-only history with instructions or tools changed through mid-conversation system messages.

claims.claim: Breaking change from Claude Sonnet 5: on the Claude API and Google Cloud, computer use works only through the computer_toolset_20260801 toolset; computer_20251124 returns a 400 error there, and computer_20250124 is not accepted on any platform.
claims.note: Quote: "On the Claude API and Google Cloud, Claude Sonnet 5.5 supports computer use only through the `computer_toolset_20260801` toolset." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: Breaking change from Claude Sonnet 5: with the advisor tool, a Claude Sonnet 5.5 executor accepts only Claude Opus 5, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5, Fable 5.1, Mythos 5, or Mythos 5.1 advisors; older advisors return a 400 error, and advice returns encrypted as an advisor_redacted_result block.
claims.note: Quote: "Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 advisors return a 400 error." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: Breaking change from Claude Sonnet 5: text longer than a sentence or two written between tool calls returns in progress-update thinking blocks, empty at the default display, instead of text blocks; no request fails, but an interface that shows those notes goes quiet. Render each non-empty thinking block before the tool_use block that follows it.
claims.note: Quote: "No request fails, but an interface that shows those notes goes quiet." Verified 2026-09-30 against the fetched vendor page by three independent skeptics in round 1 (3/3 survived).

claims.claim: Reasoning effort accepts low, medium (the default), high, xhigh, and max.
claims.note: Quote: "Set reasoning.effort to low, medium (default), high, xhigh, or max." Verified 2026-10-01.

claims.claim: The none and minimal reasoning efforts are not supported; callers that used none should start with low.
claims.note: Quote: "The none and minimal reasoning efforts are not supported."; Quote: "GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol do not support none; use low instead." Verified 2026-10-01.

claims.claim: Tool calling requires the Responses API; Chat Completions supports requests without tools.
claims.note: Quote: "Use the Responses API for tool calling. Chat Completions supports requests without tools." Verified 2026-10-01.

claims.claim: When reasoning effort is not none, remove temperature, top_p, and top_logprobs, and on Chat Completions also remove logprobs.
claims.note: Quote: "When reasoning effort is not none, remove temperature, top_p, and top_logprobs. For Chat Completions, also remove logprobs.". Stated in the migration checklist that opens with setting model to gpt-6-astra, gpt-6.1-sol, or gpt-6-luna. Verified 2026-10-01.

claims.claim: When migrating from GPT-5.5 or earlier, replace prompt_cache_retention with prompt_cache_options.ttl set to 30m.
claims.note: Quote: "When migrating from GPT-5.5 or earlier, replace prompt_cache_retention with prompt_cache_options.ttl set to "30m".". Same migration checklist as above. Verified 2026-10-01.

claims.claim: When an application changes reasoning effort between responses, use configuration_update items in standard single-agent requests and keep request-level effort unchanged to preserve the cached prefix.
claims.note: Quote: "If your application changes effort between responses, use configuration_update items in standard, single-agent requests. Keep request-level reasoning.effort unchanged to preserve the prompt prefix for caching.". Same migration checklist as above. Verified 2026-10-01.

claims.claim: The vendor positions it for complex coding, computer use, and professional work when near-Astra performance at a lower cost is wanted, and tells callers to compare it with Astra on their own tasks.
claims.note: Quote: "Use GPT-6.1 Sol for complex coding, computer use, and professional work when you want near-Astra performance at a lower cost."; Quote: "Compare it with Astra on your tasks to assess the tradeoff between quality and cost." Verified 2026-10-01.

claims.claim: Callers already on gpt-6-sol are directed to the migration guidance before switching to GPT-6.1 Sol.
claims.note: Quote: "If you already use gpt-6-sol, review the migration guidance before switching to GPT-6.1 Sol." Verified 2026-10-01.

claims.claim: The models catalog lists it at 2 US dollars per million input tokens and 10 per million output tokens, one fifth of gpt-6-astra's listed 10 and 50.
claims.note: Quote: "$2 / Input MTok"; Quote: "$10 / Output MTok"; Quote: "Near-Astra performance for complex work at a lower cost.". Astra's row on the same page lists $10 / Input MTok and $50 / Output MTok. The page states the prices, not a benchmark. Verified 2026-10-01.

claims.claim: The models catalog lists a 1.05M-token context window, 128K maximum output tokens, an April 30, 2026 knowledge cutoff, and Functions, Web search, File search, and Computer use tools, the same values as gpt-6-astra's row.
claims.note: Quote: "Near-Astra performance for complex work at a lower cost.". Row values read from the saved models.txt lines following 'Model ID gpt-6.1-sol': Max output 128K tokens; Context window 1.05M; Knowledge cutoff Apr 30, 2026. Verified 2026-10-01.

claims.claim: The guide's prompting best practices address behavior observed with GPT-6 Astra, and the vendor says to evaluate them with the chosen model; none is stated as measured on GPT-6.1 Sol.
claims.note: Quote: "They address behavior observed with GPT-6 Astra; evaluate them with your chosen model and workload." Verified 2026-10-01.

claims.claim: The guide's delegation prompt tells the model to parallelize work by delegating tasks to another agent whenever it could save time or improve quality.
claims.note: Quote withheld: it is an imperative addressed to an agent. Recorded and deliberately NOT adopted into any shared body: the catalog's agent-orchestration-primitives overrides it with the named-problem escalation gate, as for gpt-6-astra. Verified 2026-10-01.
